readAloud.text: Denim began as a tough cotton cloth produced in the French town of Nîmes, whose name gave us the phrase 'de Nîmes', later shortened to denim. In the 1870s, a Latvian tailor and a dry-goods supplier added copper rivets to strengthen work trousers, and blue jeans were born. Once clothing for miners and farmers, jeans became a global symbol of youth and casual style within a century.

Every autumn, billions of birds leave their breeding grounds in the Northern Hemisphere and travel south in search of food. Arctic terns make the longest journey of all, flying from pole to pole and cover seventy thousand kilometres a year. To navigate, birds combine cues: the position of the sun by day and the pattern of the stars by night. This remarkable ability continues to fascinate scientists.

In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements into a table by atomic weight, leaving gaps where no known element seemed to fit. He predicted that new elements would be discovered to fill those spaces, and described their properties in advance. When gallium and germanium were later found to match his predictions almost exactly, the periodic table became the foundation of modern chemistry.

Desert ants are among the most gifted navigators in the animal kingdom. After wandering hundreds of metres in search of food, a single ant walks home in an almost perfectly straight line. It achieves this by counting its steps and continuously measuring the angle it has turned relative to the sun. When researchers lengthened the ant's legs, it still overshot the nest by a predictable distance.

In 1922, the British archaeologist Howard Carter opened the tomb of Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Unlike most royal tombs, it had escaped grave robbers and still held more than five thousand objects, including the golden mask that made the boy king famous worldwide. The discovery gave historians an extraordinary picture of ancient Egyptian burial customs.

Yawning remains one of the most familiar yet least understood human behaviours. A common theory holds that yawns help cool the brain, since people yawn more often in warm rooms than in cool ones. Even more striking is contagious yawning: watching or reading about a yawn can trigger one. Psychologists link this response to empathy, noting that young children who have not yet developed it rarely catch yawns.

The pencil is a humble object with a surprisingly dramatic history. Its core is graphite, a form of carbon discovered in England in the sixteenth century, when an entire mountain of the substance was found near Keswick. Because graphite is soft and brittle, early users wrapped the sticks in string or sheepskin. Later, a German chemist mixed graphite with clay, allowing pencils to be made in different hardnesses — a formula still used worldwide today.

retellLecture.title: The Terracotta Army
retellLecture.sample: The lecture described the discovery of the Terracotta Army in 1974, when farmers digging a well near Xi'an found thousands of life-sized clay soldiers buried around 210 BC to guard the tomb of China's first emperor. No two faces are alike, and the figures once held real bronze weapons and wore bright paint, which flaked away minutes after excavation. Part of the army remains buried because conservation technology is still developing.
retellLecture.text: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an in China stumbled upon one of the greatest archaeological discoveries: the Terracotta Army. More than eight thousand life-sized clay soldiers, along with horses and chariots, had been buried around 210 BC to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China. Astonishingly, no two faces are alike, and each figure once carried real bronze weapons. The soldiers were originally painted in bright colours, but exposure to air after excavation made the paint flake away within minutes. Today, conservationists work slowly at the site, and part of the army remains buried to protect it until conservation technology improves.

retellLecture.title: Building the Great Wall
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained that the Great Wall of China is actually a series of fortifications rebuilt over two thousand years, from rammed earth in early states to brick and mortar under the Ming dynasty. Watchtowers relayed smoke warnings within hours. Contrary to popular belief, the wall never fully stopped invaders; its value lay in slowing armies, channelling them toward defended passes, and controlling trade, making communication and control as important as defence.
retellLecture.text: The Great Wall of China is not a single wall but a series of fortifications built and rebuilt over more than two thousand years. Early states used rammed earth and local stone; under the Ming dynasty, engineers added bricks and mortar, and watchtowers were positioned so that smoke signals could relay warnings between them in hours. Contrary to popular belief, the wall never stopped invaders completely; its value lay in slowing armies, channelling them toward defended passes, and giving early warning. The wall's real function was communication and control of trade as much as defence.

respondToSituation.prompt: You missed your dentist appointment yesterday because your bus broke down, and the clinic has sent a letter warning that patients who miss appointments without notice may be charged. You want to keep seeing the same dentist. Call the clinic's reception. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You missed your dentist appointment yesterday because your bus broke down, and the clinic has sent a letter warning that patients who miss appointments without notice may be charged. You want to keep seeing the same dentist. Call the clinic's reception. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hello, this is Jordan Blake, I have an appointment with Doctor Reyes. I'm calling because I missed my visit yesterday, and I feel terrible about it. My bus broke down on the way, and by the time I reached a phone, the surgery was already closed. I know the clinic charges for missed appointments, and I understand the policy — I'd be happy to pay the fee. What I'd really like is to rebook with Doctor Reyes as soon as possible, because I still need the treatment we discussed. Could you let me know the earliest available slot? I can come at any time this week. Thank you very much, and again, I'm sorry for the confusion.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: The university is considering adding a compulsory financial literacy module for all first-year students. Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students discussed a proposal to make financial literacy compulsory for first-years. Speaker A supported it strongly, arguing that many graduates accumulate debt without understanding loans, taxes, or budgeting, and that payday lenders exploit this ignorance. Speaker B objected that the curriculum is already crowded and that a one-off module would be quickly forgotten, preferring optional workshops. Speaker C proposed a short online module with practical tasks such as a budgeting simulation. They agreed that a brief, practical, compulsory online course was a reasonable compromise.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I think this is long overdue. Most of us will sign loan agreements worth thousands this year, and how many of us actually understand interest rates or how taxes work? Financial mistakes at eighteen can follow you for a decade.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I understand the motivation, but the timetable is already full. Another compulsory module means either cutting something real or overloading students. And honestly, a two-hour lecture on compound interest in week three will be forgotten by Christmas.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: What if it were online and short? A few hours of material with practical tasks — build a budget for a student loan, compare two phone contracts, spot the hidden fees in a payday loan ad. You could complete it in a week.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That would still help. The cost of not knowing this is enormous — people get trapped by payday lenders precisely because nobody taught them what the interest really means.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: If it's brief, practical, and genuinely useful — not a box-ticking lecture — I could accept making it compulsory. Make the tasks real, like planning a term's budget with our actual living costs.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: So: short online module, real-life scenarios, completed before the first loan instalment arrives. That seems like something everyone could support.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should primary schools stop setting homework? Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students discussed whether primary schools should abolish homework. Speaker A argued that young children are exhausted after a full school day and that research shows little academic benefit from homework at that age. Speaker B supported homework for building routines and involving parents, but only in small amounts, mainly daily reading. Speaker C raised the issue of unequal home environments and suggested replacing worksheets with reading and practical activities. They agreed that daily reading should remain, but formal written homework should be minimal or removed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, I'd get rid of it. Children in primary school are only young, and after six hours of lessons they need to play and rest. The research I've read says homework adds almost nothing academically at that age, but it causes plenty of evening arguments.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I see the argument, but homework isn't only about marks. Ten minutes of reading with a parent builds a routine, and it shows families what their children are learning. I'd keep that, even if we cut everything else.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: There's another problem nobody mentions: not every home is the same. Some children share a room with three siblings, or their parents work evenings. Marks-based homework ends up measuring home circumstances, not effort.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly, and that's why I'd replace worksheets with things any family can do — reading a story, cooking and measuring, that kind of task.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So daily reading stays, formal written homework goes, and anything optional is practical. That sounds like a fair balance to me.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Within seconds of meeting someone, people form judgements about trustworthiness and competence, and research shows these snap decisions are surprisingly durable. Studies find that observers agree strongly with one another about who looks friendly or capable, even when shown faces for a tenth of a second. Such judgements are shaped by facial structure, clothing, posture, and voice, and they influence real outcomes: interviewers favour candidates who appear confident, and voters often support candidates who simply look competent. Critics argue that these impressions are frequently wrong, because they rely on superficial cues rather than actual behaviour. Nevertheless, first impressions are difficult to overturn, since later information tends to be interpreted in ways that confirm the initial judgement. For this reason, communication experts advise preparing carefully for first encounters.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: First impressions form within seconds, are shaped largely by superficial cues, and strongly influence real outcomes such as hiring and voting; although they are often inaccurate, they persist because later information is interpreted to confirm them, so experts advise preparing carefully for first encounters.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Procrastination is often misunderstood as laziness, but psychologists describe it as a problem of emotion regulation rather than time management. When a task triggers anxiety, boredom, or self-doubt, delaying it provides immediate relief, and the brain learns to repeat the pattern. Unfortunately, avoidance increases stress as deadlines approach, and the task itself becomes even more threatening. Research suggests that breaking projects into small, specific steps reduces the emotional barrier, because starting is the hardest part. Self-compassion also helps: students who forgive themselves for procrastinating procrastinate less afterwards, while harsh self-criticism deepens the cycle. Deadlines imposed by others help only partially, since the underlying emotions remain. Effective strategies therefore focus on lowering the cost of beginning rather than on willpower alone.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Psychologists view procrastination as emotion regulation rather than laziness, since delaying anxiety-inducing tasks brings relief that reinforces avoidance; effective responses include breaking work into small steps and practising self-compassion, which lower the emotional cost of starting, whereas harsh self-criticism and external deadlines help little.

essay.prompt: In some countries, voting in national elections is compulsory; in others, voting is voluntary. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of compulsory voting and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.
essay.sample: Possible structure: (1) Introduction — outline the debate (compulsory vs voluntary voting) and state your position. (2) Advantages: higher and more representative turnout, elections reflect the whole population rather than only motivated voters, reduces the influence of extreme groups that mobilise small bases, easier campaigning focused on policies. (3) Disadvantages: personal freedom arguments — voting as a right, not a duty; uninformed or resentful votes may distort results; fines punish the poor disproportionately. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. compulsory voting is justified because democratic legitimacy outweighs the freedom argument, possibly with a 'none of the above' option. Useful phrases: 'It is widely debated whether…', 'A frequently cited advantage is…', 'Critics counter that…', 'Weighing both sides, I would argue…'

Together with his brother Jacques-Étienne, he built a paper-lined fabric balloon and filled it with hot air from a burning fire of straw and wool. summarizeSpokenText.title: Recording without writing: the Inca quipu
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture explained how the Inca empire kept detailed records without writing, using the quipu — coloured cords hung with smaller strings and knots. The position, colour, and type of knot encoded numbers such as crops stored, taxes owed, and population figures for whole provinces. Because the code has never been fully deciphered, scholars debate whether quipu also recorded stories or songs. The speaker concluded that the quipu proves a civilisation can organise information without literacy.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: The Inca empire ruled millions of people without any known system of writing, yet its administrators kept remarkably detailed records. Their tool was the quipu, a set of coloured cords from which smaller strings hung, each decorated with knots. The position, colour, and type of knot encoded numbers: crops stored, taxes owed, and population figures for entire provinces. Because the code has never been fully deciphered, scholars debate whether quipu also recorded stories or songs. Whatever the answer, the quipu shows that a sophisticated civilisation can organise information without a single written sentence — a useful reminder that literacy is not the only path to administration.

summarizeSpokenText.title: A short history of ice cream
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture traced ice cream from its ancient roots, when Chinese and Persian cooks mixed snow with fruit syrups and chilled dairy, to the iced desserts served by European nobility, which demanded huge stores of ice. The modern cone appeared by accident at the 1904 World's Fair when vendors ran out of dishes and borrowed waffles from a neighbouring stall. Industrial refrigeration then turned the luxury into an everyday treat, illustrating how technologies invented for the wealthy eventually become affordable for everyone.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Ice cream has surprisingly ancient roots. Chinese and Persian cooks were mixing snow with fruit syrups and chilled dairy more than a thousand years ago, and European nobility later impressed guests with iced desserts that required enormous quantities of stored ice. The modern cone appeared at the 1904 World's Fair in America, where vendors ran out of dishes and borrowed thin waffles from a neighbouring stall. Industrial refrigeration then turned a luxury into an everyday treat. The speaker ends by noting that ice cream illustrates a familiar pattern: technologies invented for the wealthy eventually become affordable for everyone.
